items.text: Hash map get and put are O(1) on average but O(n) worst case when keys collide into one bucket; Java 8+ HashMap caps that at O(log n) by turning long buckets into trees.
Appending to a dynamic array is amortized O(1): capacity doubles when full, so n appends copy at most about 2n elements in total.
Inserting or deleting at the front of an array is O(n) because every element shifts; a deque (ring buffer) gives O(1) operations at both ends.
A balanced BST gives O(log n) search, insert, delete and in-order iteration; a hash table is faster on average but loses key ordering.
Linked lists offer O(1) insert and delete at a known node but O(n) access by index, and their poor cache locality often makes them slower than arrays.
log2 of one billion is about 30, so binary search over a billion sorted items needs at most around 30 comparisons.
Rule of thumb: about 10^8 simple operations per second. For n = 10^5, O(n log n) is instant, but O(n^2) = 10^10 operations will time out.
Comparison sorting has an Omega(n log n) lower bound: there are n! possible orderings, and a decision tree needs log2(n!), about n log n, levels to tell them apart.
Building a heap bottom-up (heapify) is O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes sit near the bottom and sift down only a few levels.
In Python, 'x in list' is O(n) but 'x in set' is O(1) on average; converting a list to a set first can turn an O(n^2) loop into O(n).
Quicksort averages O(n log n) but degrades to O(n^2) on sorted input with a naive first or last pivot; random or median-of-three pivots avoid this.
Merge sort is O(n log n) in every case and stable, but the array version needs O(n) extra memory for merging.
Heapsort is O(n log n) worst case and in place with O(1) extra space, but it is not stable and has poor cache behavior.
A stable sort keeps equal elements in their original order, so sorting by a secondary key and then by the primary key yields a correct multi-key sort.
Counting sort runs in O(n + k) where k is the key range; great for small integer ranges like ages or exam scores, useless for arbitrary 64-bit keys.
LSD radix sort sorts integers digit by digit with a stable counting sort per digit, running in O(d * (n + b)) for d digits in base b.
Timsort (Python, Java for objects) detects existing sorted runs and merges them: stable, O(n log n) worst case, and O(n) on already sorted data.
Introsort (typical C++ std::sort) starts as quicksort, switches to heapsort when recursion gets too deep, and uses insertion sort for tiny ranges.
Insertion sort is O(n^2) but very fast on small or nearly sorted arrays, which is why hybrid sorts use it for partitions under about 16 to 32 elements.
Quickselect finds the k-th smallest element in O(n) average time by partitioning like quicksort but recursing into only one side.
External merge sort handles data larger than RAM: sort memory-sized chunks and write them to disk, then k-way merge the chunks with a min-heap.
Count inversions in O(n log n) during merge sort: whenever you take an element from the right half, add the number of elements left in the left half.
Binary search: compute mid as lo + (hi - lo) / 2 instead of (lo + hi) / 2 to avoid integer overflow in fixed-width languages.
Lower bound (first index with a[i] >= target) on a half-open range [lo, hi): if a[mid] < target then lo = mid + 1, else hi = mid.
Binary search on the answer: if feasibility is monotonic (works for x implies works for x + 1), binary search x itself, e.g. the minimum ship capacity.
In a rotated sorted array, at least one half around mid is always sorted; check whether the target lies inside that half to choose a side.
Find a peak element in O(log n): if a[mid] < a[mid + 1], a peak exists to the right; otherwise one exists at mid or to its left.
Python's bisect_left and bisect_right return the first index >= x and > x; their difference counts the occurrences of x in a sorted list.
Exponential search doubles an index (1, 2, 4, 8, ...) until it passes the target, then binary searches that range: O(log i) for target position i.
Search a matrix sorted by rows and columns in O(m + n): start at the top-right corner, move left if the value is too big, down if too small.
Two Sum on a sorted array: start pointers at both ends, move left forward if the sum is too small and right backward if too big. O(n) time, O(1) space.
3Sum in O(n^2): sort, fix one element, then run a two-pointer scan on the rest; skip equal neighbors to avoid duplicate triplets.
Floyd's cycle detection: a slow pointer moving 1 step and a fast pointer moving 2 steps will meet inside a cycle if one exists, using O(1) memory.
After Floyd's slow and fast pointers meet, reset one to the head and advance both 1 step at a time; they meet again at the start of the cycle.
Container With Most Water: always move the pointer at the shorter line inward, since moving the taller one can never increase the area.
Trapping Rain Water in O(1) space: two pointers track leftMax and rightMax, and you process the side with the smaller max, since it bounds the water there.
Sliding window: grow the right edge to add elements and shrink the left edge while the window is invalid; each element enters and leaves once, so O(n).
Longest substring without repeating characters: store each char's last index and move left to max(left, last[c] + 1). One pass, O(n).
Minimum window substring: count the needed characters, track how many are satisfied, and shrink from the left whenever all of them are covered.
Sliding windows solve 'longest subarray with sum <= k' only when all numbers are nonnegative; negatives break the shrink rule, so switch to prefix sums.
Exactly K distinct = atMost(K) - atMost(K - 1): turning an exact-count window problem into two at-most windows makes it straightforward.
Prefix sums: with P[i] = a[0] + ... + a[i-1], the sum of a[l..r] is P[r+1] - P[l], answered in O(1) after O(n) setup.
Count subarrays summing to k in O(n): keep a hash map of prefix-sum counts and add count[prefix - k] at each step. Seed it with count[0] = 1.
2D prefix sums: rectangle sum = P[r2][c2] - P[r1][c2] - P[r2][c1] + P[r1][c1] with half-open bounds, by inclusion-exclusion.
Difference array: to add v to a[l..r], do d[l] += v and d[r+1] -= v; a single prefix sum at the end applies all q range updates in O(n + q).
Next greater element in O(n): keep a stack of indices with decreasing values; pop while the current value is larger and record it as their answer.
Largest rectangle in a histogram uses an increasing monotonic stack: when a bar is popped, its width spans from the new stack top to the current index.
Sliding window maximum in O(n): keep a deque of indices with decreasing values; pop the back while smaller, and pop the front once it leaves the window.
A hash table stays fast by bounding its load factor; Java's HashMap resizes at 0.75 full so chains stay short and operations stay O(1) on average.
Open addressing stores entries in the array itself and probes on collision; linear probing is cache friendly but suffers from primary clustering.
Deleting from an open-addressing hash table needs tombstones; simply emptying the slot would break probe sequences for keys inserted after it.
Group anagrams by a canonical key: the sorted string, or a tuple of 26 letter counts to skip the O(L log L) sort.
Consistent hashing places servers and keys on a ring, so adding or removing one of n servers remaps only about 1/n of the keys.
Hash-flooding attacks craft colliding keys to make hash tables O(n) per operation, which is why Python and Rust use keyed hashes like SipHash.
Top K largest of n items: keep a min-heap of size k and pop whenever it exceeds k. O(n log k) time and O(k) memory, ideal for streams.
Running median: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, kept within one element in size; the median sits at the tops.
Merge k sorted lists in O(N log k): push each list's head into a min-heap, pop the smallest, then push the next element from that list.
Binary heap as an array: the children of index i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and its parent is (i - 1) / 2. No pointers needed.
Most binary heaps lack decrease-key, so Dijkstra implementations push duplicate entries and skip stale ones when popped (lazy deletion).
An in-order traversal of a BST visits keys in sorted order, which makes 'k-th smallest element' a simple in-order walk that stops at k.
Validate a BST by passing (min, max) bounds down the recursion; comparing each node only with its direct children misses deeper violations.
A BST built by inserting sorted input degenerates into a linked list with O(n) operations; self-balancing trees keep height O(log n).
AVL trees keep sibling subtree heights within 1, giving slightly faster lookups; red-black trees allow height up to 2 log2(n + 1) but rotate less on writes.
Red-black trees back Java's TreeMap and typical C++ std::map: ordered keys, O(log n) operations, and floor or ceiling queries.
B-trees pack many keys per node so a lookup touches few disk pages; with a fanout of 100, three levels already index about a million keys.
B+ trees keep all values in leaves linked in key order, making range scans fast; that is why most database indexes use them.
A trie looks up a word or prefix in O(L) for key length L, no matter how many words it stores, which makes it ideal for autocomplete.
Segment tree: O(log n) range queries (sum, min, max) and point updates in about 4n memory; lazy propagation adds O(log n) range updates.
Fenwick tree (BIT): prefix sums and point updates in O(log n) with an array of n + 1 values, stepping with i += i & -i to update and i -= i & -i to query.
Lowest common ancestor in a binary tree: recurse into both children; if both calls return non-null, the current node is the LCA.
Tree diameter: the longest path through a node is leftHeight + rightHeight, so track the max of that while computing heights in a single DFS.
BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs in O(V + E); DFS does not, even though it visits the same nodes.
0-1 BFS: when edge weights are only 0 or 1, use a deque, pushing 0-weight neighbors to the front and 1-weight ones to the back. O(V + E).
Dijkstra with a binary heap runs in O((V + E) log V) but requires nonnegative edge weights; a single negative edge can produce wrong answers.
Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge V - 1 times in O(VE); if one more pass still shortens a distance, the graph has a reachable negative cycle.
A* is Dijkstra ordered by f = g + h; an admissible heuristic h (one that never overestimates) guarantees an optimal path, and h = 0 is plain Dijkstra.
Kahn's topological sort: repeatedly remove nodes with in-degree 0; if some nodes are never removed, the graph contains a cycle.
DFS topological sort outputs nodes in reverse post-order; reaching a node that is still on the recursion stack (a back edge) means there is a cycle.
Union-Find with path compression and union by rank does each operation in O(alpha(n)) amortized, where alpha(n) is below 5 for any practical n.
Kruskal's MST: sort edges by weight and add each one unless Union-Find says its endpoints are already connected. O(E log E).
Prim's MST grows a single tree, always adding the cheapest edge leaving it: O(E log V) with a binary heap, or O(V^2) with an array for very dense graphs.
The cut property justifies Kruskal and Prim: the lightest edge crossing any cut of the graph belongs to some minimum spanning tree.
Strongly connected components: Tarjan's algorithm finds them all in one DFS using low-link values; Kosaraju uses two DFS passes, one on the reversed graph.
Collapsing each strongly connected component into one node always yields a DAG, so many directed-graph problems become DP in topological order.
Floyd-Warshall computes all-pairs shortest paths in O(V^3) with three nested loops; the intermediate-vertex loop k must be the outermost.
Bipartite check: 2-color the graph with BFS or DFS; an edge between two nodes of the same color reveals an odd cycle, so it is not bipartite.
Grid problems are graphs: each cell is a node with up to 4 neighbors, so counting islands is counting connected components with BFS or DFS.
Multi-source BFS: enqueue every source at distance 0 up front to get each cell's distance to its nearest source in a single O(V + E) pass.
Mark nodes visited when you enqueue them in BFS, not when you dequeue them; otherwise the same node can be added to the queue many times.
Shortest paths in a DAG work even with negative weights: relax edges in topological order for O(V + E), no Dijkstra needed.
Dynamic programming fits problems with optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems: define the state, the transition, and the base cases.
Memoization (top-down) computes only the states you actually reach; tabulation (bottom-up) avoids recursion limits and makes space optimization easy.
0/1 knapsack in a 1D array: loop capacity from high to low so each item is used at most once; looping low to high gives unbounded knapsack instead.
Longest increasing subsequence in O(n log n): tails[i] holds the smallest tail of any increasing subsequence of length i + 1; binary search each value's slot.
LCS: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 if the characters match, else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). O(mn) time, O(min(m, n)) space with rolling rows.
Edit distance: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] if the chars match, else 1 + min(delete dp[i-1][j], insert dp[i][j-1], replace dp[i-1][j-1]).
Interval DP (matrix chain, burst balloons): dp[i][j] over subarrays, filled by increasing length while trying every split point k. Usually O(n^3).
When a DP row depends only on the previous row, keep just two rows (or one), cutting memory from O(nm) to O(m).
Coin change (fewest coins) is unbounded knapsack: dp[x] = min(dp[x], dp[x - coin] + 1). Greedy fails for coins {1, 3, 4} and target 6.
Bitmask DP handles subsets of up to about 20 items: TSP with dp[mask][last] runs in O(2^n * n^2) instead of trying all n! routes.
Kadane's algorithm finds the maximum subarray sum in O(n): cur = max(x, cur + x) and best = max(best, cur) at each element.
Longest palindromic substring: expand around each of the 2n - 1 centers for O(n^2) time and O(1) space; Manacher's algorithm does it in O(n).
Knapsack's O(nW) is pseudo-polynomial: polynomial in the value of W, but exponential in the number of bits needed to write W down.
Interval scheduling: to fit the most non-overlapping intervals, always pick the one that ends earliest; an exchange argument proves it optimal.
Exchange argument: to prove a greedy choice, take any optimal solution and show that swapping in the greedy choice never makes it worse.
Minimum meeting rooms: sort meetings by start and keep a min-heap of end times; the largest heap size reached is the number of rooms needed.
Huffman coding repeatedly merges the two least frequent symbols, and this greedy process yields an optimal prefix-free code.
Fractional knapsack is solved greedily by value-to-weight ratio, but 0/1 knapsack is not; greedy fails once items cannot be split.
Jump Game: track the farthest reachable index while scanning; if the current index ever exceeds it, the end is unreachable. O(n).
Backtracking template: choose, recurse, un-choose. Prune as early as possible when a partial solution can no longer lead to a valid answer.
Know your search spaces: 20 items have 2^20 (about a million) subsets but 20! (about 2.4 * 10^18) permutations.
N-Queens prunes quickly by tracking used columns and both diagonals in sets: r - c identifies one diagonal and r + c the other.
To avoid duplicate combinations when the input has repeats, sort first and skip nums[i] when i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1].
x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit, so x is a power of two exactly when x > 0 and x & (x - 1) == 0.
x & -x isolates the lowest set bit in two's complement; Fenwick trees use it to jump between nodes.
XOR all the numbers to find the single element that appears once when every other appears twice, since a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a.
Kernighan's popcount: repeat x &= x - 1 until x is 0; the number of iterations equals the number of set bits.
Enumerate all non-empty submasks of mask with for (s = mask; s > 0; s = (s - 1) & mask); summed over all masks this is O(3^n).
With 32-bit ints, 1 << 31 hits the sign bit and 1 << 32 is undefined in C (Java wraps it to 1); use 1L << k in Java or 1ULL << k in C.
A Bloom filter answers 'maybe present' or 'definitely absent' with k hashes over a bit array: false positives are possible, false negatives are not.
Bloom filter sizing: about 10 bits per element with 7 hash functions gives roughly a 1% false-positive rate.
HyperLogLog estimates distinct counts from the longest runs of leading zeros in hashes; Redis uses 12 KB per key for about 0.81% standard error.
Count-Min sketch estimates frequencies with d rows of w counters and takes the minimum across rows; it may overestimate but never underestimates.
Reservoir sampling keeps k uniform random items from a stream of unknown length: keep the first k, then item i replaces a random slot with probability k/i.
Skip lists stack sorted linked lists, promoting each node to higher levels at random, for expected O(log n) search; Redis sorted sets use them.
Fisher-Yates shuffle: for i from n - 1 down to 1, swap a[i] with a[rand(0..i)]; swapping with rand(0..n-1) every time produces a biased shuffle.
KMP precomputes a failure table (longest proper prefix that is also a suffix) so matching never steps backward in the text: O(n + m).
Rabin-Karp compares a rolling hash of each text window to the pattern's hash in O(1) per shift, verifying characters only on a hash match.
Z-algorithm computes Z[i], the longest prefix match starting at i, in O(n); to search, build it on pattern + '$' + text and look for Z[i] == m.
Aho-Corasick adds failure links to a trie to match many patterns at once in O(text length + total pattern length + matches).
Accounting method: charge each cheap operation a little extra credit, and show the saved credit always pays for the occasional expensive one.
Queue from two stacks: push onto 'in', pop from 'out', and refill 'out' from 'in' only when it is empty. Each element moves once, so O(1) amortized.
Amortized is not average case: amortized O(1) is a guarantee over any sequence of operations, while average case depends on the input distribution.
Interview heuristic: sorted input suggests binary search or two pointers, 'top k' suggests a heap, and 'all combinations' suggests backtracking.
Read constraints as hints: n up to 10^5 rules out O(n^2), n <= 20 invites O(2^n), and n <= 10 allows O(n!).
Say the brute force first: it gives you a correct baseline and its complexity, and often reveals exactly which step to optimize.
Need fast lookup of 'what have I seen so far'? Reach for a hash map; many O(n^2) pair searches become O(n) this way.
Stuck on a tree or graph problem? Decide exactly what each recursive call returns to its parent; that definition usually unlocks the solution.
Python's default recursion limit is 1000, so recursive DFS on a long path crashes; use an explicit stack or raise the limit with care.
Dry-run your solution on edge cases before declaring it done: empty input, one element, all duplicates, negatives, and the maximum size.
